rv.q: The Wild West looms large in American self-mythology.
But in the end, it is too cluttered — stylistically, tonally, ideologically — to offer much insight.
But the fact that their own thematically comparable show contributes so little of substance to the same grand, gnarly conversation is their pig and their farm .
Dark Noon is a frenetic, triumphant production that is both hugely entertaining and deeply thought-provoking for American audiences in particular.
As of now, both High Noon and Dark Noon are must-sees, the former as perfect of its kind, the latter flawed but endlessly insistent
If nothing else, it’s one of the most gleefully provocative pieces of theater you’ll see this year.
Dark Noon has two problems: There is no point of focus in its staging and no point of focus in its satirical point of view.
The production is also American in the extreme, mining veins of joyfulness and hope amid repeating cycles of violence.
It’s jaw-droppingly audacious, and breathtakingly fearless, daring you to either look away or challenge what you’re seeing.
Dark Noon is an energetic juggernaut, but one wishes the show had a more discerning eye.

cn.t: South African actors deliver an energetic, provocative reimagining of Wild West history, but critics are divided: some praise its fresh outsider perspective while others find it overbuilt and unfocused.
